title: Torn anterior cruciate ligament (ACL)
intro: The anterior cruciate ligament is a strong band inside the knee that keeps the shin bone from sliding forward and stabilises rotation. Tearing it often happens during sport, with a sudden twist or landing awkwardly, and can cause the knee to give way. Treatment may be exercise-based or surgical depending on your activities.

sections.heading: How it happens
paragraphs: ACL tears usually happen without contact, when someone changes direction quickly, stops suddenly or lands from a jump, as in football, basketball, skiing and handball. Women have a higher risk. People often feel or hear a pop, followed by rapid swelling and a sense that the knee is unstable.

sections.heading: Symptoms and diagnosis
paragraphs: Pain, swelling within hours, difficulty putting weight on the leg and instability or giving way are typical. Doctors examine the knee with special tests of laxity and usually obtain an MRI scan to confirm the tear and check for other injuries such as meniscus damage. X-rays exclude fractures.

sections.heading: First steps
paragraphs: Rest the knee, apply cold packs, compression and elevation, and use crutches while pain is severe. Painkillers help. Gentle movement and physiotherapy start early to restore range of motion and reduce swelling, since a stiff knee can make later surgery or recovery harder.

sections.heading: Exercise-based treatment or surgery
paragraphs: Many people manage well without surgery, especially if they do not need to twist and pivot in sport. Structured physiotherapy strengthens the muscles to stabilise the knee, and surgery can be done later if the knee keeps giving way. Studies show similar results at two to five years in many patients between early surgery and rehabilitation with optional later surgery. Surgery, in which the ligament is replaced with a graft usually taken from the patient's own tendon, is more often advised for young athletes in pivoting sports, for people whose knee gives way in daily life and for those with other injuries in the knee.

sections.heading: Recovery
paragraphs: After surgery, rehabilitation lasts about nine to twelve months before returning to pivoting sports. Return depends on strength, balance and confidence, not just time on the calendar. Re-tear risk is highest in young athletes who return early. Prevention programmes with strengthening and landing technique reduce injury risk. An ACL injury raises the risk of knee osteoarthritis over time.

examples.title: Weighing options
examples.text: Imagine you play football weekly and tore your ACL. You could discuss both surgery and structured rehabilitation with your surgeon and ask what return to sport would involve.

examples.title: Preparing for surgery
examples.text: Suppose you decide on surgery. You might begin physiotherapy beforehand to regain movement and strength, and plan time off work.
